title: A Thursday special: Responding to Charles R's reflections about understanding
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton answers a friend who accuses him of dodging a firm definition of understanding. He defends a deliberately ambiguous working definition, arguing that understanding is ambiguous by nature, citing Andras Schiff and Wiggins and McTighe as evidence that even experts hedge. He accepts his friend's view that understanding emerges from knowledge, skills and reflection, but stresses that it develops far more slowly and is less controllable than either. He also argues that brain development and assessment-driven schooling work against early teaching for understanding, and that schools should stop pretending to assess it as they assess knowledge. He closes with a working definition of understanding as a personal, slowly changing big picture, and a poem on seeing the particular and the universal together.
points: Understanding is ambiguous by nature, so a definition that keeps some ambiguity is accurate rather than evasive.
Knowledge, skills and understanding differ in timescale: knowledge sticks quickly, skills more slowly, and understanding slowest and least controllable.
Developmental limits and assessment-driven systems both work against early teaching for understanding, and Wiggins and McTighe concede it is only one aim among many.
Schools should stop expecting test-style results from understanding while still valuing it as personal and slow to emerge.
quotes: It is the ambiguity, by the way, that means you keep going back to the set of posts about ‘Understanding’ rather than those about ‘Knowledge’. It's this ambiguity that is behind Andreas Schiff saying he 'thinks he understands’ Bach's Goldberg Variations now. The important word here is, of course, 'thinks' rather than 'understands'.

I can't accurately describe the wonderful stroganoff I ate recently by simply retelling what the ingredients were or what the chef did with them. The stroganoff 'transcends and includes' the ingredients and the chef’s skills but ends up as something different that I can't quite put into words. Understanding is different to this, of course, but the metaphor will do for now.

Our brain development and the system both work against the early introduction of understanding. The good news is that this may not matter as much as some people who want to encourage understanding too early may think.

your deepening of understanding will happen even more slowly, emerge from your reflection and never quite be sticky, even to yourself, let alone me. We do have some control over the knowledge you learn or the skills we acquire. We don’t have the same control over what understandings we will deepen.

We live in a world where clarity and 'knowing' have become elevated to the top spot and where 'not knowing' and lack of clarity get short shrift. This is why social media works so well; everybody shouts their knowledge at each other as quickly as possible.

I agree with Wiggins and McTighe. I'm in the paradoxical position of believing that deepening our personal understandings is vital but that schools should stop pretending they are teaching for understanding when it is inappropriate and stop expecting the same kind of analysable test results from student understanding as they do from knowledge and skills, when there isn't a hope in hell of this being able to happen.

Understanding seems to be the personal, slowly changing, slightly ungraspable big picture or pictures we make for ourselves of our own - and others - lives. It emerges slowly when our experiences, our knowledge and abilities, our personalities and our predilections are put into the pot and allowed to simmer over time. It's this that makes understanding significantly different from knowledge and skills.
